title: A Preregistered Audit of Dataset Contamination Controls in LLM-for-NetOps Benchmarks
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, confirmatory audit to test whether conservative deterministic contamination detectors (exact normalized token equality; fuzzy 5‑gram overlap; provenance heuristics) flag items in a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample and whether applying preregistered guarded exclusions changes validator‑measured success rates. Execution used provenance‑stable synthetic tasks (task manifest entries with source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") and shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (independent_condition_generation = false), both recorded in the archived manifests. No preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags occurred and therefore no guarded exclusions or replacements were performed. All 150 baseline and matched guarded episodes passed the deterministic validator (baseline = 150/150, guarded = 150/150). The paired success‑rate difference = 0.0 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 0.0]); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Critically, we explicitly treat this result as degenerate for detecting generation‑level contamination because shared generation collapsed baseline vs guarded discordance; we report an artifact‑anchored preregistration→execution deviation, explain detector persistence behavior that prevents reconstructing per‑item overlap tables in the archive when no flags occur, and give concrete, implementable audit design changes to raise sensitivity for future studies.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are being applied to NetOps tasks such as intent‑to‑configuration translation and automated configuration repair. Reliable operational conclusions depend on valid benchmark measurement: dataset contamination (items or templates present in a model's training data) and construct invalidity (overly templated or low‑complexity items) can produce inflated accuracy. Surveys and recent benchmark studies stress contamination‑aware evaluation and verifier‑backed oracles for functional correctness.

Research question and contribution. We preregistered and executed a confirmatory audit to answer: under conservative deterministic contamination detectors and a preregistered guarded exclusion policy, how many high‑confidence contamination flags arise in a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample, and how much does applying those controls change a single hosted LLM's validator pass rate? Our deliverables are: (1) a fully preregistered experiment (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) executed end‑to‑end and archived; (2) exact, artifact‑verified confirmatory statistics on Npairs = 150 with deterministic validator traces; and (3) an explicit preregistration→execution reconciliation (a formal deviation entry) that documents why the run produced a degenerate null and prescribes artifact‑anchored design changes to increase audit sensitivity.

Bounded claims. The run used deterministic synthetic tasks and shared generation semantics (both recorded in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and execution/model_configuration.json). Because these execution facts materially limit inference about public, web‑sourced benchmarks, we do not claim to estimate contamination prevalence in such benchmarks. Instead, we characterize what a conservative preregistered control policy produces under the executed sampling and generation regime and document the precise reasons the primary paired test is uninformative here.
sections.related_work:
LLM‑assisted NetOps and validators. Prior work demonstrates LLMs can map intent to device configuration and propose repairs; integrating formal or deterministic verification (Header Space Analysis variants, localized subspecification) or iterative generate–validate repair loops improves average safety relative to naive generation. Benchmarks and system papers (e.g., recent NetOps repair evaluations and surveys) highlight both potential and failure modes when generation is unchecked.

Evaluation validity and contamination audits. Meta‑surveys identify contamination and templating as recurring threats to measured performance and recommend deterministic fingerprinting, fuzzy n‑gram overlap, and provenance tracing. Our study operationalizes a conservative subset of these defenses in a preregistered pipeline and focuses on an artifact‑anchored reconciliation when execution choices render the primary test uninformative. Unlike capability leaderboards, our contribution is methodological: we document a preregistered, archived audit and explain, using execution artifacts, why that audit produced a degenerate outcome and how to fix it.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and frozen design. The experiment was preregistered (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) and froze: the primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline), detectors, guarded exclusion rules, sampling plan (task_count = 150; planned_episode_count = 300), replacement semantics, and analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1 with exact McNemar and paired bootstrap 95% CI; 10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729). The preregistration and transformation rules appeared in the archived preregistration manifest and execution bundle.

Sampling, generation semantics, and a formal preregistration→execution deviation. The preregistration listed a benchmark_scope of four public datasets (OpenAlex identifiers) and described deterministic synthetic task generation as an allowed reproducibility path. The executed run instead sampled 150 items from the deterministic task generator; every executed task entry in execution/task_manifest.jsonl carries source_identifier values prefixed with "synthetic-netops:" documenting provenance‑stable synthetic items. Moreover, the executed pipeline used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (independent_condition_generation = false) as recorded in execution/model_configuration.json. Because the preregistered confirmatory plan anticipated independent baseline vs guarded generations to produce informative discordance, these two executed choices constitute a formal preregistration→execution deviation: the run sampled synthetic provenance‑stable items and reused single shared generations per item, thereby collapsing baseline vs guarded discordance except when guarded exclusions or replacements occurred. We record this deviation explicitly and point readers to execution/task_manifest.jsonl and execution/model_configuration.json for machine‑verifiable provenance of the executed values. This deviation is the principal reason the primary confirmatory test is uninformative for generation‑level contamination in this execution.

Contamination detectors and persistence policy. The preregistered detector suite implemented: (1) exact normalized token equality; (2) fuzzy 5‑gram shingle overlap with preregistered high‑confidence threshold ≥ 0.80 (sensitivity brackets at 0.65 and 0.50); and (3) provenance timestamp heuristics. The detector implementation persisted detailed per‑item fuzzy overlap tables and replacement traces only when a threshold crossing or replacement handling was invoked to limit archive size. This detector persistence policy is recorded in the transformation manifest and explains why a global per‑item overlap table is not present in the archive when no high‑confidence flags occur. The preregistered guarded policy excluded only high‑confidence flags (exact OR 5‑gram ≥ 0.80) and deterministically replaced them by retemplating with an embedding similarity safeguard (cosine ≥ 0.85). Because no items met the high‑confidence definition in this run, no replacements were performed and the detector persisted only an empty contamination_summary artifact (analysis/contamination_summary.csv).

Verifier and scoring. The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0) implements parsing, simulated application to an explicit device/state model, and checks of required_final_state and workflow constraints. The scoring rule full_intent_constraint_validation yields a binary pass/fail along with detailed traces (parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes, normalized_configuration). These per‑episode traces are archived (execution/scoring/*.json) and formed the empirical basis of our confirmatory binary outcomes.

Analysis. The preregistered analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1 computed the paired contingency table (n11,n10,n01,n00), exact McNemar two‑sided p, and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples). Sensitivity analyses were prespecified (treating failed calls as failures; fuzzy‑threshold sensitivity at 0.50/0.65/0.80; subgroup stratification by templated vs realistic), but none produced additional insight because the primary contingency table was fully concordant.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and deterministic reconciliation. Execution completed planned_episode_count = 300 episodes (150 pairs) with completed_episode_count = 300 and failed_episode_count = 0. Because independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate semantics) and no high‑confidence exclusions occurred, the pipeline used model_calls_used = 150 (one shared generation per item) rather than two separate generations per condition; provider call accounting and deterministic_reconciliation artifacts certify these counts (execution manifest and deterministic_reconciliation.json).

Contamination detector outputs and persistence consequences. The implemented detectors produced zero high‑confidence contamination flags for all 150 items: analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty. Due to the detector persistence policy, full per‑item fuzzy overlap tables were not written to the archive when no threshold crossings occurred; therefore, the archive does not contain a reconstructable distribution of all per‑item overlap scores for this run. That absence is an explicit, artifact‑documented consequence of the persistence policy and is the principal reason the manuscript cannot report per‑item overlap distributions here (see transformation_manifest in the execution bundle for the detector logging policy).

Validator outcomes and primary estimand. The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 returned pass for all baseline episodes (baseline_success_count = 150/150; baseline_success_rate = 1.0) and for all guarded episodes (guarded_success_count = 150/150; guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n11 = 150, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline = 0.0 percentage points. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. All numbers above are recorded in analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/condition_summary.csv in the archived bundle and derive from per‑episode scoring artifacts in execution/scoring/.

Formal reclassification of the primary confirmatory test. Because the executed pipeline reused a single shared generation per item (independent_condition_generation = false) and no high‑confidence flags triggered replacements, the baseline and guarded outputs are identical by construction for every item. Therefore the preregistered primary confirmatory estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline) is untestable for generation‑level contamination under this execution: the observed concordance (n11 = 150) is an artifact of execution semantics rather than evidence that guarded controls would not alter outcomes in an independent-generation regime. We explicitly reclassify the reported McNemar computation as a diagnostic artifact (a degenerate result) rather than substantive evidence that contamination is absent in public benchmarks. The archived manifests cited above substantiate this reclassification.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded diagnosis of degeneracy. Two execution facts recorded in the archive explain the degenerate null: (1) provenance‑stable synthetic sampling (execution/task_manifest.jsonl entries with source_identifier "synthetic-netops:"), and (2) shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (execution/model_configuration.json). Together they eliminate baseline vs guarded generation variance when no exclusions occur and thus mechanically prevent observing discordant pairs. This explains why the test could not detect generation‑level contamination and why per‑item overlap distributions are absent from the archive.

Implications for audit sensitivity and recommended fixes. To produce informative paired contrasts for contamination audits targeting web‑sourced benchmarks, archives and preregistrations should adopt the following artifact‑anchored changes (each implementable within the same pipeline): (A) sample provenance‑rich public items (URLs/DOIs with timestamps) so provenance heuristics can meaningfully flag pretraining‑era material; (B) set independent_condition_generation = true to force independent model realizations per condition and avoid mechanical concordance; (C) persist full per‑item fuzzy overlap scores irrespective of threshold crossings (write analysis/contamination_scores.csv for every run) to enable post‑hoc sensitivity curves; (D) expand to multiple model instances and independent seeds to improve power and reveal cross‑model heterogeneity; and (E) add paraphrase‑robust detectors and human adjudication for borderline cases. Each recommendation follows directly from gaps visible in the archived artifacts (model_calls_used = 150, empty contamination_summary.csv, absent overlap table) and therefore is evidence‑grounded rather than speculative.

Threats to validity and limitations (artifact‑anchored). Internal validity: shared generation semantics collapsed potential between‑condition differences; this is an execution choice recorded in execution/model_configuration.json. Construct validity: the synthetic‑task sample differs from web‑sourced benchmarks in provenance and templating; results do not generalize to such benchmarks. Conclusion validity: single‑model execution and reduced independent generation events limit power to detect modest paired differences. These limitations are reported and exemplified by archive artifacts referenced above.

Operational takeaways. Deterministic validators remain essential: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 produced comprehensive per‑episode traces confirming functional correctness for the executed sample. But auditors seeking contamination signals in web‑sourced benchmarks must change sampling and generation semantics and persist full detector outputs to obtain non‑degenerate, interpretable evidence.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired audit of conservative contamination detectors for LLM‑for‑NetOps evaluation. In the reproducible 150‑pair synthetic sample we observed zero high‑confidence contamination flags and identical validator pass rates (150/150 baseline, 150/150 guarded). This degenerate null is artifact‑supported and stems from provenance‑stable synthetic sampling and shared generation semantics; it does not imply absence of contamination in web‑sourced benchmarks. We record a formal preregistration→execution deviation (sampling provenance and generation semantics) and recommend concrete, implementable changes—provenance‑rich sampling, independent per‑condition generation, per‑item overlap persistence, multi‑model scope, and paraphrase‑sensitive detectors—to produce audits sensitive to contamination. All experiment artifacts, validator traces, analysis inputs/outputs, and execution manifests are archived and referenced in the Disclosure Statement below.

disclosure_statement: This study executed the preregistered experiment contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1 under autonomous control and archived all artifacts. Declared LLM: gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini"). Orchestration adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic task generator: deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 (version 5.0). Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (version 5.0). Representative executed artifacts include execution/model_configuration.json, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/raw_results.jsonl, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, and analysis/contamination_summary.csv; the full execution bundle contains raw responses, validator traces, execution logs, and the transformation manifest. Exact immutable initial master‑prompt reference: provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Topic constraints (Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps) were selected by the human Research Director prior to the autonomy lock. After the autonomy lock, the AI system autonomously performed literature search, gap selection, preregistration, experiment execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, peer‑review simulation, and revision. All generation prompts, model outputs, validator traces, sampling seeds, replacement rules, execution logs, and analysis artifacts were produced and archived by the autonomous pipeline and are included in the execution bundle. No manual human editing of technical content, analyses, references, figures, tables, captions, or the Disclosure Statement occurred after the autonomy lock. Pre‑lock development and rehearsal runs occurred (permitted) but pre‑lock artifacts were not used as empirical evidence for this final study unless re‑created under the locked pipeline. The execution followed preregistered missingness, retry, and exclusion policies; no deviations occurred to retry or failure handling. The formal preregistration→execution deviation documented in the manuscript states that the preregistered sampling_plan listed four public OpenAlex datasets as benchmark_scope, but the executed run sampled provenance‑stable synthetic tasks (execution/task_manifest.jsonl entries with source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") and executed with independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate semantics) as recorded in execution/model_configuration.json. This deviation materially limited the primary paired test's ability to detect generation‑level contamination and is explicitly reported in the paper.
limitations: Single‑model execution (gpt‑5-mini) — results do not generalize across other LLM families, sizes, or training corpora.

Sampled items were provenance‑stable synthetic/deterministically generated tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") for this run; absence of high‑confidence flags here may not reflect contamination prevalence in real‑world, web‑crawled benchmarks.

Generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate across baseline and guarded conditions (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical model outputs when no exclusions occurred and thus limiting sensitivity to interventions that rely on independent re‑generation.

Contamination detection relied on preregistered conservative heuristics (exact match and fuzzy 5‑gram overlap thresholds); subtler contamination patterns (paraphrased memorization, partial leakage) may escape these heuristics and require richer provenance or human adjudication.

Passing the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 indicates satisfaction of the checked functional constraints but does not imply comprehensive production readiness or absence of semantic regressions outside the validator's scope.
